newsitem.title: USA: Rapid pace of U.S utility mergers set to continue.
newsitem.headline: Rapid pace of U.S utility mergers set to continue.

text.p: Large U.S. utility mergers, like the proposed combination of Pacific Enterprises and ENOVA Corp, will continue as the electric industry moves toward open competition, industry officials said.
"We are going to see a lot of mergers in this industry, " Daniel Scotto, senior managing director of Bear, Stearns & Co told an electric utility conference here.

"We may be returning to a time when we have a number of larger holding companies," Scotto said, referring to the 1970s and earlier when the electric industry was dominated by fewer, primarily monopolistic, companies.
Under deregulation, electric utilities were mandated to offer transmission services to independent generators for the same price they charge themselves, opening the market to more competition.
Officials said the new rules will continue to pressure utilities to seek combinations and alliances to raise capital and improve operating efficiency.

Pacific Enterprises, the parent of natural gas distribution company Southern California Gas Co, and Enova, the parent of San Diego Gas and Electric Co, said Monday they plan to merge their operations.

"The size of recent electricity mergers and alliances with gas companies is virtually unprecedented," James Hoecker, commissioner with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), told the conference, which was sponsored by Bear, Stearns and law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges.
Hoecker said electricity and natural gas mergers worth about $1 trillion have been transacted over the past 21 months, with $152 billion worth of mergers in the third quarter of this year.
"Are we going to see market dominance by a few utilities? That is a concern," Hoecker said.
The FERC is working on new merger review legislation to replace a merger review process which is "unpardonably long," Hoecker said.
Although the FERC expects new merger legislation, a government official said the U.S. Congress was not likely to act soon to pass deregulation or utility merger legislation.

"We do not yet fully understand what the situation is in regards to electricity," said U.S. House of Representatives member John Dingell (D-Mich), adding the newly-competitive market needs to settle out before government action is taken.
-- Chris Reese, New York Power Desk 212-859-1627
